newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries steady in London, await payrolls.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries steady in London, await payrolls.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries in London were little changed in modest volumes on Thursday ahead of a crucial U.S. June employment report due later, analysts said.
On Wednesday the market took no heart from Federal Reserve's widely expected decision to kept interest rates unchanged. Analysts said that prospect was still intact for the coming months.
"Obviously there were no surprises last night. But we are still concerned about course of Fed policy going forward," said Philip Tyson, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.
"Rates will go up either in August or September and even today payrolls have the potential to unnerve Treasuries."
At 0919 GMT, the U.S. long bond was at 98-28 to yield 6.71 percent, compared with 98-30 in Tokyo, 98-28 at Wednesday's New York close.
Two-year T-notes were at 99-31, unchanged from the Tokyo and New York closes while 10-year T-notes were also unchanged from Tokyo at 101-19, one tick higher from New York.
The U.S. June employment report is due at 1230 GMT. A Reuters consensus of economists' forecasts expected non-farm payrolls to rise to 222,000 compared with a rise of 138,000 in May.
The unemployment rate was forecast to remain unchanged at 4.8 percent while average hourly earnings were expected to rise slightly to 0.4 percent from 0.3 percent.
Tyson said the payrolls figure would be the highlight of the day, and a strong number could rattle the market. HSBC Markets forecast the figure to come in around 280,000.

"The report has the potential to worry the market and we will probably look for yields to end up higher on the day," he said, but added that the rise in yields could be limited ahead of a long weekend in the U.S.
The U.S. will be closed on Friday to mark the Independence Day.
Charles Quigley, U.S. bond salesman at Chase in London, was more optimistic on the employment report.
"It probably isn't a day of reckoning," he said. "Important as the employment numbers are, the question in the short-term is what do they mean for Federal Reserve policy. And the answer is nothing."

Quigley said even if the Fed had had some inkling of what the data were, politically and economically it had so far been correct not to tighten interest rates just because the labour market was tight.
He said inflation had not got any worse, and the cycle of a strong employment report and bond sell-off followed by good inflation news and a rally, had now passed.
"A strong labour report could bring a modest down tick, but investors are still inclined to be buyers and prices don't stay down very long," he said.
Conversely, if the number was weaker than expected the longer end of yield curve could quickly re-price itself to yield around 6-5/8 to 6-1/2 percent, he said.
Quigley said activity had concentrated so far on the two-year sector, with some interest in 10-year paper as well.
September T-bond futures were at 112-04, up 2/32 from Wednesday's Chicago settlement.
--Deepthi Wickremasinghe, Bonds Unit +44 171 542 4041
